# Manual tariff recipes

A multiplicative tariff is a **decision object**: after the fitted model, an
actuary may revise selected factors deliberately. Azoic supports that without
a new model class — `extract_tariff` decomposes a fitted log-link GLM into a
factor dictionary, `apply_tariff` scores a (possibly edited) dictionary, and
`recalibrate_for_total` shifts the base to restore a portfolio total.

Treat judgemental factor changes as a **revised tariff**, not a tweak of the
fitted model: editing the dictionary does not update the fitted pipeline or a
previously exported workbook, and changing bin boundaries or group membership
requires refitting the downstream model. Record the original factors and the
reasons for each change.

{{< include _shared.qmd >}}

```{python}
from azoic.tariff import extract_tariff, recalibrate_for_total

portfolio = load_portfolio()
glm_config, _ = make_experiment_configs(str(PORTFOLIO_PATH))
glm_config = glm_config.model_copy(
    update={"models": {"direct-tweedie-glm": glm_config.models["direct-tweedie-glm"]}}
)
glm_run, glm_estimators = run_experiment(glm_config, return_estimators=True)
train_frame = portfolio.iloc[list(glm_run.train_indices)].copy()
test_frame = portfolio.iloc[list(glm_run.test_indices)].copy()
y_train = train_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_train = train_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()
y_test = test_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_test = test_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()

glm_pipeline = glm_estimators["direct-tweedie-glm"]
fitted_preprocessing = glm_pipeline[:-1]
fitted_glm = glm_pipeline[-1]
special_predict_columns = [*FEATURES, "exposure", "claim_amount", "claim_count"]
transformed_test = fitted_preprocessing.transform(test_frame[special_predict_columns])
```

## Extract and reproduce

`extract_tariff` returns `base_rate` (intercept folded with reference-level
coefficients), per-unit numeric coefficients, categorical relativities against
a chosen reference level, and a mapping table. Applying the untouched
dictionary on the same transformed features reproduces the fitted prediction.

```{python}
tariff = extract_tariff(fitted_glm)
model_rate = np.asarray(glm_pipeline.predict(test_frame[[*FEATURES, "exposure"]]), dtype=float)
applied_rate = apply_tariff(tariff, transformed_test)
np.testing.assert_allclose(applied_rate, model_rate, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-8)
display(pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "base_rate": [tariff["base_rate"]],
        "numeric_features": [len(tariff["numeric"])],
        "categorical_features": [len(tariff["categorical"])],
    }
))
display(tariff["mapping"].head(15))
```

## Revise one factor, then restore the total

Below, one grouped level of `region` gets a deliberate +10% factor. This
local change affects only that segment and can change ranking between policies.
The original training O/P is already close to, but not exactly, one (about
0.99817 with the default data); the edit changes that level further.

`recalibrate_for_total` then supplies a new base rate that balances the edited
tariff to observed training claims. This second step is a common positive
multiplier: it preserves the edited tariff's ranking, not necessarily the
original model's ranking. We put the new base into a separate dictionary and
freeze it for testing; neither the fitted model nor a workbook is updated.

```{python}
revised = {
    "base_rate": tariff["base_rate"],
    "numeric": dict(tariff["numeric"]),
    "categorical": {feat: dict(levels) for feat, levels in tariff["categorical"].items()},
}
feature = "region"
levels = revised["categorical"][feature]
edited_level = next(level for level, factor in levels.items() if not np.isclose(factor, 1.0))
levels[edited_level] *= 1.10

original_op = op_ratio(y_train, np.asarray(glm_pipeline.predict(
    train_frame[[*FEATURES, "exposure"]]), dtype=float), w_train)
transformed_train = fitted_preprocessing.transform(train_frame[special_predict_columns])
revised_rate_train = apply_tariff(revised, transformed_train)
revised_op = op_ratio(y_train, revised_rate_train, w_train)
assert abs(revised_op - original_op) > 1e-3

new_base = recalibrate_for_total(
    revised,
    predicted_total=float(revised_rate_train @ w_train),
    observed_total=float(y_train.sum()),
)
revised_recalibrated = {**revised, "base_rate": new_base}
restored_rate_train = apply_tariff(revised_recalibrated, transformed_train)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    op_ratio(y_train, restored_rate_train, w_train), 1, rtol=0, atol=1e-10
)
display(pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "variant": ["fitted GLM", "edited factor", "edited + recalibrated"],
        "training_O/P": [
            original_op,
            revised_op,
            op_ratio(y_train, restored_rate_train, w_train),
        ],
    }
))
```

The same totals check belongs on the held-out rows: recalibrating to training
totals fixes the training level but does not claim to fix test calibration or
any segment-level bias.

```{python}
restored_rate_test = apply_tariff(revised_recalibrated, transformed_test)
display(pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "variant": ["fitted GLM", "edited factor", "edited + recalibrated"],
        "test_O/P": [
            op_ratio(y_test, model_rate, w_test),
            op_ratio(y_test, apply_tariff(revised, transformed_test), w_test),
            op_ratio(y_test, restored_rate_test, w_test),
        ],
        "test_deviance": [
            mean_tweedie_deviance(y_test / w_test, model_rate, sample_weight=w_test, power=1.5),
            mean_tweedie_deviance(
                y_test / w_test, apply_tariff(revised, transformed_test),
                sample_weight=w_test, power=1.5,
            ),
            mean_tweedie_deviance(
                y_test / w_test, restored_rate_test, sample_weight=w_test, power=1.5,
            ),
        ],
    }
))
```

For changes to model flexibility or sparse-risk pooling, return to
[the experiment controls](02-experiments.qmd#regularization-controls).
Choose those settings inside training data. Revisions prompted by the inspected
holdout need fresh evaluation data; this illustration does not provide it.
